Hand-verified cases, using the observation that the LCS with a string over a single repeated letter is the count of that letter in T, capped at N. The "ab" length-3 case rests on a hand count of 76 strings containing "ab" as a subsequence, which I did not re-verify by a second method.

```json
[
  {"input": "1 1\na", "output": "25 1"},
  {"input": "1 2\na", "output": "625 51"},
  {"input": "2 1\nab", "output": "24 2 0"},
  {"input": "2 2\naa", "output": "625 50 1"},
  {"input": "3 1\nabc", "output": "23 3 0 0"},
  {"input": "1 3\nb", "output": "15625 1951"},
  {"input": "3 2\naaa", "output": "625 50 1 0"},
  {"input": "2 3\nab", "output": "13824 3676 76"},
  {"input": "2 3\naa", "output": "15625 1875 76"},
  {"input": "2 2\nba", "output": "576 99 1"}
]
```

These were worked out by hand, not by running a program. The key facts used: for M=1 the LCS is at most 1, and a single letter has LCS 1 exactly when it appears in S. For length-M strings with S having distinct letters, LCS ≥ 1 iff the string shares a letter with S. For LCS ≥ 2 with S = "ab", the count of length-3 strings containing "ab" as a subsequence is 76, via the standard formula Σ_{j=n}^{M} C(j−1, n−1)(q−1)^{j−n} q^{M−j}.

These cases are small enough to verify by hand. Each output sums to 26^M, and I checked the counts by classifying strings by letter content (or, for "ab" with M=3, by a greedy subsequence automaton).
